meta.title: MCP Question Bank — Chapter 8 (Multi-Select): Security & Trust
meta.format: multi_select: questions use the 'answers' array (multiple correct options). Some include an 'All of the above' option that is only correct when every other option is.

questions.question: Which risks does the token passthrough anti-pattern create? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Circumvention of security controls like rate limiting and traffic monitoring that depend on token audience
Loss of accountability: downstream logs attribute requests to the wrong identity
The server becoming a proxy for data exfiltration with stolen tokens
Trust-boundary breakage: a token accepted by multiple services lets one compromise spread
Improved latency due to skipped validation

questions.explanation: All four risks are documented reasons the spec forbids passthrough. 'Improved latency' is not a recognized benefit — validation must happen.

questions.question: Which SSRF mitigations should server-deployed MCP clients implement when fetching OAuth-related URLs? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Require HTTPS, allowing http:// only for loopback during development
Validate redirect targets with the same rules instead of blindly following them
Hand-roll custom IP-parsing validation to catch encoding tricks
Consider egress proxies (e.g., Smokescreen) that block internal destinations by design

questions.explanation: A, B, C, and E are the documented mitigations. D is explicitly warned against: avoid manual IP validation, since attackers exploit octal/hex/IPv4-mapped-IPv6 encodings that custom parsers miss.

questions.question: Before executing a one-click local MCP server configuration, the client MUST... (Select all that apply.)

options.text: show the exact command that will be executed, without truncation
clearly identify it as a potentially dangerous operation that executes code
require explicit user approval before proceeding
allow the user to cancel
upload the command to a central review service first

questions.explanation: The four MUSTs are full command display, danger identification, explicit approval, and cancellation. Central review is not required (sandboxing and dangerous-pattern warnings are SHOULDs).

questions.question: Which of these are listed as common scope-design MISTAKES? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Publishing all possible scopes in scopes_supported
Using wildcard or omnibus scopes like *, all, or full-access
Bundling unrelated privileges to preempt future prompts
Emitting precise scope challenges instead of the full catalog
Treating claimed scopes in a token as sufficient without server-side authorization logic

questions.explanation: A, B, C, and E are on the common-mistakes list. Emitting precise challenges (D) is the recommended behavior, not a mistake.

questions.question: Which mitigations does the security-best-practices doc give for the confused deputy problem? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Obtain per-client user consent — do not rely on a consent cookie set for a different dynamically-registered client
Treat a static client ID fronting many downstream clients as a high-risk pattern
Validate redirect URIs strictly against registered values
Skip the consent screen for returning users to reduce friction
All of the above

questions.explanation: The attack works precisely because a cached consent cookie skips the screen while the attacker swaps in their redirect URI. D is the vulnerability, not the mitigation.

questions.question: Which statements about server-minted state handles (the 2026-07-28 replacement for sessions) are true? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A handle is NOT proof of identity — authorization must come from the verified token on each request
Handles should be generated with secure randomness, not guessable sequences
Servers should bind stored state to the authenticated user (e.g., key by user_id:handle) so a stolen handle is useless cross-user
A handle may safely double as a bearer credential since it's random
All of the above

questions.explanation: Random ≠ authorization: the doc's core rule is that handles reference state while the token authorizes. Treating the handle as a credential recreates session hijacking.

questions.question: Which claims must a resource server verify on an inbound access token? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The signature, against the issuer's published keys
The expiry (exp)
The audience (aud) — the token was issued for THIS server
The issuer (iss) — a trusted authorization server
All of the above

questions.explanation: Signature, expiry, audience, and issuer together are the minimum bar; audience validation is what kills token passthrough. All true, so E holds.

questions.question: Which URL-scheme rules apply when a client opens an OAuth authorization URL? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Only http:// and https:// URLs may be opened
The URL must never be passed to a shell or interpreted as a command
Custom schemes like myapp:// from an untrusted server should be rejected for the authorization step
javascript: URLs are acceptable if the authorization server is trusted
All of the above

questions.explanation: javascript: (and file:, custom schemes) in an attacker-influenced URL is an execution vector — exactly what the rule exists to block.
